questions.question: Which load balancing algorithm distributes requests evenly in sequence across all servers?
questions.explanation: Round-robin sends requests to servers in rotation: 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3... It's simple and works well when servers have equal capacity and requests have similar processing times.

questions.question: A backend has servers with different capacities: Server A can handle 3x the load of Server B. Which algorithm best utilizes this?
questions.explanation: Weighted round-robin assigns weights to servers (e.g., A=3, B=1), sending proportionally more traffic to higher-capacity servers. Plain round-robin would underutilize Server A.

questions.question: Which algorithm is best when request processing times vary significantly?
questions.explanation: Least connections routes to the server with fewest active connections. When processing times vary, this prevents slow requests from causing one server to accumulate a backlog.

questions.question: A gaming application needs players from the same IP to always connect to the same server for session consistency. Which algorithm achieves this?
questions.explanation: IP hash uses the client's IP address to deterministically select a server. The same IP always maps to the same server, providing session persistence without cookies.

questions.question: What is a disadvantage of the IP hash algorithm?

options.text: Users behind NAT/proxy share an IP, causing uneven distribution

questions.explanation: Many users behind corporate NAT or proxies share the same public IP. IP hash would send all of them to the same server, causing uneven load distribution.

questions.question: Which load balancing algorithms provide session persistence? (Choose all that apply)
questions.explanation: IP hash and cookie-based persistence ensure the same client reaches the same server. Round-robin and least connections distribute without client affinity.

questions.question: A load balancer uses 'least response time' algorithm. What does it optimize for?

options.text: Server that responded fastest to recent health checks

questions.explanation: Least response time routes to servers responding fastest, combining connection count with response latency. It adapts to real-time server performance rather than just connection count.

questions.question: True or False: Round-robin is always the best algorithm for evenly distributing load.
questions.explanation: Round-robin distributes requests evenly but not necessarily load. If some requests take longer, servers can become unbalanced. Least connections often provides better actual load distribution.

questions.question: A microservices architecture uses service mesh with client-side load balancing. Which algorithm works well for this?
questions.explanation: P2C randomly picks two servers and chooses the one with fewer connections. It's efficient for distributed/client-side LB—no central state needed, yet better than random.

questions.question: Which factors should influence load balancing algorithm selection? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: The programming language of backend services

questions.explanation: Server capacity affects weighted vs unweighted algorithms. Session needs affect persistence algorithms. Processing time variability affects round-robin vs least-connections. Programming language is irrelevant.

questions.question: What is 'consistent hashing' in the context of load balancing?

options.text: Ensuring all servers receive exactly equal traffic
A hash-based algorithm that minimizes redistribution when servers change

questions.explanation: Consistent hashing maps requests to servers such that adding/removing a server only affects a small portion of requests. It's useful for caching layers where redistribution causes cache misses.

questions.question: A load balancer is configured with 'least bandwidth' algorithm. What does it measure?

options.text: Server with lowest network interface speed
Server currently serving least amount of traffic (Mbps)

questions.explanation: Least bandwidth routes to the server currently handling the least traffic volume (bytes/second). Useful when requests vary significantly in response size (e.g., file downloads).
